/-!
# (Exponential) periods

Kontsevich and Zagier define a *period* as a complex number whose real and imaginary parts are
values of absolutely convergent integrals of rational functions with rational coefficients over
domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$ given by polynomial inequalities with rational coefficients. The
periods form a countable ring $\mathcal{P}$ with
$\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \subset \mathcal{P} \subset \mathbb{C}$. Allowing the integrand to also
contain the exponential of an algebraic function gives the ring of *exponential periods*
$\mathcal{EP}$.

Wikipedia lists the open problem "Which transcendental numbers are (exponential) periods?". The
concrete conjectures recorded there, going back to Kontsevich and Zagier, are that $1/\pi$,
Euler's number $e$ and the Euler–Mascheroni constant $\gamma$ are not periods. Both $e$ and
$\gamma$ are known to be exponential periods.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Period (algebraic geometry)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Period_%28algebraic_geometry%29)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [KZ01] Kontsevich, M., Zagier, D., *Periods*. In: Mathematics Unlimited — 2001 and Beyond,
  Springer, 2001, pp. 771–808.
- [La13] Lagarias, J. C., *Euler's constant: Euler's work and modern developments*.
  Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 50 (2013), 527–628. [arXiv:1303.1856](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.1856)
- [MS14] Müller-Stach, S., *What is a period?*. Notices Amer. Math. Soc. 61 (2014).
  [arXiv:1407.2388](https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.2388)
-/

def IsRatSemialgebraic {n : ℕ} (D : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  D ∈ BooleanSubalgebra.closure {s | ∃ p : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℚ, s = {x | 0 ≤ aeval x p}}
blocks.docstring:
A subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is *semialgebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$* if it belongs to the Boolean
algebra of sets generated by the sets $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid p(x) \geq 0\}$ with
$p \in \mathbb{Q}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. These are the domains "given by polynomial inequalities
with rational coefficients" in the definition of a period.

justification.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib has no semialgebraic sets (rg for 'semialgebraic' in Mathlib and FormalConjecturesForMathlib returned nothing); `BooleanSubalgebra.closure` (Mathlib.Order.BooleanSubalgebra) is used to build it.
justification.name: ExponentialPeriods.IsRatSemialgebraic
justification.why_needed: The Kontsevich–Zagier definition integrates over domains in ℝ^n 'given by polynomial inequalities with rational coefficients', i.e. ℚ-semialgebraic sets. Mathlib has no notion of semialgebraic set. Defined as membership in `BooleanSubalgebra.closure` of the sets `{x | 0 ≤ aeval x p}` for `p : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℚ`, which is the standard Boolean-algebra definition of semialgebraic sets (strict inequalities arise as complements).

blocks.name: IsRatSemialgebraic
blocks.text:
/--
A subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is *semialgebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$* if it belongs to the Boolean
algebra of sets generated by the sets $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid p(x) \geq 0\}$ with
$p \in \mathbb{Q}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. These are the domains "given by polynomial inequalities
with rational coefficients" in the definition of a period.
-/
def IsRatSemialgebraic {n : ℕ} (D : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  D ∈ BooleanSubalgebra.closure {s | ∃ p : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℚ, s = {x | 0 ≤ aeval x p}}

def IsRealPeriod (a : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (n : ℕ) (D : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) (f g : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℚ),
    IsRatSemialgebraic D ∧ IntegrableOn (fun x => aeval x f / aeval x g) D ∧
      a = ∫ x in D, aeval x f / aeval x g
blocks.docstring:
A real number $a$ is a *period* (Kontsevich–Zagier) if it is the value of an absolutely
convergent integral
$$a = \int_D \frac{f(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}{g(x_1, \ldots, x_n)} \, dx_1 \cdots dx_n$$
of a rational function $f / g$ with $f, g \in \mathbb{Q}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ over a domain
$D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ that is semialgebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$.

Absolute convergence is encoded by `IntegrableOn` with respect to Lebesgue measure on
`Fin n → ℝ`. Lean's convention `x / 0 = 0` is harmless: for `g ≠ 0` the zero set of `g` is
Lebesgue-null, and for `g = 0` the integral is `0`, which is a period.

justification.closest_existing_considered: `RatFunc` (one variable only, so unsuitable); `MvPolynomial` + `aeval` used for the numerator/denominator instead.
justification.name: ExponentialPeriods.IsRealPeriod
justification.why_needed: No notion of Kontsevich–Zagier period exists in Mathlib or the repository (rg for 'IsPeriod', 'Kontsevich', 'Zagier' finds nothing relevant). A real `a` is a period iff `∃ n D f g, IsRatSemialgebraic D ∧ IntegrableOn (fun x => aeval x f / aeval x g) D ∧ a = ∫ x in D, aeval x f / aeval x g` with `f g : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℚ` and `volume` the Lebesgue measure on `Fin n → ℝ`; `IntegrableOn` encodes absolute convergence.

blocks.name: IsRealPeriod
blocks.text:
/--
A real number $a$ is a *period* (Kontsevich–Zagier) if it is the value of an absolutely
convergent integral
$$a = \int_D \frac{f(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}{g(x_1, \ldots, x_n)} \, dx_1 \cdots dx_n$$
of a rational function $f / g$ with $f, g \in \mathbb{Q}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ over a domain
$D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ that is semialgebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$.

Absolute convergence is encoded by `IntegrableOn` with respect to Lebesgue measure on
`Fin n → ℝ`. Lean's convention `x / 0 = 0` is harmless: for `g ≠ 0` the zero set of `g` is
Lebesgue-null, and for `g = 0` the integral is `0`, which is a period.
-/
def IsRealPeriod (a : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (n : ℕ) (D : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) (f g : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℚ),
    IsRatSemialgebraic D ∧ IntegrableOn (fun x => aeval x f / aeval x g) D ∧
      a = ∫ x in D, aeval x f / aeval x g

def IsPeriod (z : ℂ) : Prop :=
  IsRealPeriod z.re ∧ IsRealPeriod z.im
blocks.docstring: A complex number is a *period* if its real and imaginary parts are (real) periods.

justification.name: ExponentialPeriods.IsPeriod
justification.why_needed: Kontsevich–Zagier define periods as complex numbers whose real and imaginary parts are real periods; `IsPeriod z := IsRealPeriod z.re ∧ IsRealPeriod z.im`. The API lemma `isPeriod_ofReal_iff` (proved) checks that for a real number this agrees with `IsRealPeriod`.

A complex number is a *period* if its real and imaginary parts are (real) periods.

@[category test, AMS 11 14]
theorem isRealPeriod_ratCast (q : ℚ) : IsRealPeriod q := by
  refine ⟨0, Set.univ, C q, 1, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · exact BooleanSubalgebra.top_mem
  · simp
  · simp [integral_const, Measure.real, volume_pi]
blocks.docstring: Every rational number is a period: integrate the constant $q$ over $\mathbb{R}^0$.
blocks.name: isRealPeriod_ratCast
blocks.text:
/-- Every rational number is a period: integrate the constant $q$ over $\mathbb{R}^0$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11 14]
theorem isRealPeriod_ratCast (q : ℚ) : IsRealPeriod q := by
  refine ⟨0, Set.univ, C q, 1, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · exact BooleanSubalgebra.top_mem
  · simp
  · simp [integral_const, Measure.real, volume_pi]

@[category API, AMS 11 14]
theorem isPeriod_ofReal_iff (a : ℝ) : IsPeriod a ↔ IsRealPeriod a := by
  have h0 : IsRealPeriod 0 := by simpa using isRealPeriod_ratCast 0
  simp [IsPeriod, h0]
blocks.docstring: A real number is a period as a complex number if and only if it is a real period.
blocks.name: isPeriod_ofReal_iff
blocks.text:
/-- A real number is a period as a complex number if and only if it is a real period. -/
@[category API, AMS 11 14]
theorem isPeriod_ofReal_iff (a : ℝ) : IsPeriod a ↔ IsRealPeriod a := by
  have h0 : IsRealPeriod 0 := by simpa using isRealPeriod_ratCast 0
  simp [IsPeriod, h0]

@[category research open, AMS 11 14]
theorem exponential_periods.parts.i : ¬ IsPeriod (1 / π) := by
  sorry
blocks.docstring:
**Conjecture (Kontsevich–Zagier).** The number $1 / \pi$ is not a period.

Since $\pi$ is a period, this says that $\pi$ is not a unit in the ring of periods
$\mathcal{P}$; equivalently, the ring of extended periods $\hat{\mathcal{P}}$, obtained by
adjoining $1 / \pi$, is strictly larger than $\mathcal{P}$.

claims.decomposer_note: Reading for the Kontsevich–Zagier ring of periods P: the deliverable is a description of the set {x transcendental | x is a period}, and no candidate description is asserted in the statement or any background source (only special-case conjectures below), so there is no definite Prop; note 'transcendental' is automatically implied by non-membership since Q̄ ⊂ P.

Parenthetical reading for the larger ring of exponential periods EP (integrand = algebraic function × exp of algebraic function over semialgebraic domain): again a description deliverable; the sources only record known members (e, γ, √π, Γ(p/q) ∈ EP) and assert no conjecture about which transcendental numbers fail to be exponential periods, so nothing to formalize.

Prop: 1/π is not a period (Kontsevich–Zagier §1.1; equivalently π is not a unit in P, or 1/(2πi) ∉ P as Lagarias phrases it); needs a bespoke `IsPeriod` definition (absolutely convergent integral of a rational function with rational coefficients over a domain cut out by polynomial inequalities with rational coefficients, complex numbers via real and imaginary parts); the 'transcendental' qualifier is redundant since algebraic numbers are periods.
claims.reviewer_why: `¬ IsPeriod (1 / π)` (elaborates to `1 / (↑Real.pi : ℂ)`, equal to `↑(1/π)`), with the bespoke Kontsevich–Zagier `IsPeriod` (real and imaginary parts are absolutely convergent Lebesgue integrals of `f/g`, `f g ∈ ℚ[x₁..xₙ]`, over ℚ-semialgebraic sets = Boolean algebra generated by `{p ≥ 0}`). All 8 candidates state the same proposition; c07's definition uses the standard rigorous reading of 'domain given by polynomial inequalities' (Yoshinaga, Commelin–Habegger–Huber, Huber–Müller-Stach), which is the most inclusive class and is the one proven in the literature to give the ring 𝒫. Docstrings lightly edited; the `x/0 = 0` note from c04/c05 added to the `IsRealPeriod` docstring.

claims.decomposer_note: Prop: e = exp 1 is not a period (conjecture from Kontsevich–Zagier §1.1, cited via Lagarias and Müller-Stach); contrast with the known fact e ∈ EP, which is why it is expected that P ⊊ EP.
claims.reviewer_why: `¬ IsPeriod (exp 1)` with `exp = Real.exp` coerced to ℂ, i.e. e is not a period, under the same `IsPeriod`. Correctly does not claim anything about exponential periods (e ∈ EP is known).

claims.decomposer_note: Prop: Real.eulerMascheroniConstant is not a period (Lagarias Conjecture 2 / Kontsevich–Zagier §1.1); it would imply γ is transcendental, and γ is known to be an exponential period, so no exponential-period counterpart is conjectured.
claims.reviewer_why: `¬ IsPeriod eulerMascheroniConstant` with Mathlib's `Real.eulerMascheroniConstant` coerced to ℂ, under the same `IsPeriod`. Citation corrected to Lagarias [La13, Conjecture 1.2] (numbering in the arXiv source).

context:
In mathematics, specifically number theory, a period or algebraic period is a complex number that can be expressed as an integral of an algebraic function over an algebraic domain. The periods are a class of numbers which includes, alongside the algebraic numbers, many well known mathematical constants such as the number π. Sums and products of periods remain periods, so that the periods ${\mathcal {P}}$ form a ring.
Maxim Kontsevich and Don Zagier gave a survey of periods and introduced some conjectures about them. 
Periods play an important role in the theory of differential equations and transcendental numbers as well as in open problems of modern arithmetical algebraic geometry. They also appear when computing the integrals that arise from Feynman diagrams, and there has been intensive work trying to understand the connections.

decomposition_objections.text: None. The table's three Props match the sentence 'It is conjectured that 1/π, Euler's number e and the Euler–Mascheroni constant γ are not periods' in the Wikipedia article and Kontsevich–Zagier §1.1 (as cited by Lagarias and Müller-Stach). Dropping the open-ended question 'Which transcendental numbers are (exponential) periods?' is correct: it has no statable Prop.

/-!
# (Exponential) periods

Kontsevich and Zagier define a *period* as a complex number whose real and imaginary parts are
values of absolutely convergent integrals of rational functions with rational coefficients over
domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$ given by polynomial inequalities with rational coefficients. The
periods form a countable ring $\mathcal{P}$ with
$\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \subset \mathcal{P} \subset \mathbb{C}$. Allowing the integrand to also

$\gamma$ are known to be exponential periods.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Period (algebraic geometry)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Period_%28algebraic_geometry%29)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [KZ01] Kontsevich, M., Zagier, D., *Periods*. In: Mathematics Unlimited — 2001 and Beyond,
  Springer, 2001, pp. 771–808.
- [La13] Lagarias, J. C., *Euler's constant: Euler's work and modern developments*.
  Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 50 (2013), 527–628. [arXiv:1303.1856](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.1856)
- [MS14] Müller-Stach, S., *What is a period?*. Notices Amer. Math. Soc. 61 (2014).
  [arXiv:1407.2388](https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.2388)
-/

namespace ExponentialPeriods

open MeasureTheory MvPolynomial Real

/--
A subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is *semialgebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$* if it belongs to the Boolean
algebra of sets generated by the sets $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid p(x) \geq 0\}$ with
$p \in \mathbb{Q}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. These are the domains "given by polynomial inequalities
with rational coefficients" in the definition of a period.
-/
def IsRatSemialgebraic {n : ℕ} (D : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  D ∈ BooleanSubalgebra.closure {s | ∃ p : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℚ, s = {x | 0 ≤ aeval x p}}

/--
A real number $a$ is a *period* (Kontsevich–Zagier) if it is the value of an absolutely
convergent integral
$$a = \int_D \frac{f(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}{g(x_1, \ldots, x_n)} \, dx_1 \cdots dx_n$$
of a rational function $f / g$ with $f, g \in \mathbb{Q}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ over a domain
$D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ that is semialgebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$.

Absolute convergence is encoded by `IntegrableOn` with respect to Lebesgue measure on
`Fin n → ℝ`. Lean's convention `x / 0 = 0` is harmless: for `g ≠ 0` the zero set of `g` is
Lebesgue-null, and for `g = 0` the integral is `0`, which is a period.
-/
def IsRealPeriod (a : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (n : ℕ) (D : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) (f g : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℚ),
    IsRatSemialgebraic D ∧ IntegrableOn (fun x => aeval x f / aeval x g) D ∧
      a = ∫ x in D, aeval x f / aeval x g

/--
A complex number is a *period* if its real and imaginary parts are (real) periods.
-/
def IsPeriod (z : ℂ) : Prop :=
  IsRealPeriod z.re ∧ IsRealPeriod z.im

/-- Every rational number is a period: integrate the constant $q$ over $\mathbb{R}^0$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11 14]
theorem isRealPeriod_ratCast (q : ℚ) : IsRealPeriod q := by
  refine ⟨0, Set.univ, C q, 1, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · exact BooleanSubalgebra.top_mem
  · simp
  · simp [integral_const, Measure.real, volume_pi]

/-- A real number is a period as a complex number if and only if it is a real period. -/
@[category API, AMS 11 14]
theorem isPeriod_ofReal_iff (a : ℝ) : IsPeriod a ↔ IsRealPeriod a := by
  have h0 : IsRealPeriod 0 := by simpa using isRealPeriod_ratCast 0
  simp [IsPeriod, h0]

/--
**Conjecture (Kontsevich–Zagier).** The number $1 / \pi$ is not a period.

Since $\pi$ is a period, this says that $\pi$ is not a unit in the ring of periods
$\mathcal{P}$; equivalently, the ring of extended periods $\hat{\mathcal{P}}$, obtained by
adjoining $1 / \pi$, is strictly larger than $\mathcal{P}$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11 14]
theorem exponential_periods.parts.i : ¬ IsPeriod (1 / π) := by
  sorry

/--
**Conjecture (Kontsevich–Zagier).** Euler's number $e$ is not a period.

Since $e$ is known to be an exponential period, this would show that the ring of periods is
strictly smaller than the ring of exponential periods.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11 14]
theorem exponential_periods.parts.ii : ¬ IsPeriod (exp 1) := by
  sorry

/--
**Conjecture (Kontsevich–Zagier; Lagarias [La13, Conjecture 1.2]).** The Euler–Mascheroni
constant $\gamma$ is not a period.

Since every algebraic number is a period, this would imply that $\gamma$ is transcendental.
Note that $\gamma$ is known to be an exponential period.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11 14]
theorem exponential_periods.parts.iii : ¬ IsPeriod eulerMascheroniConstant := by

items: Definition of period follows Kontsevich–Zagier (as quoted in Lagarias arXiv:1303.1856 §3.14, Müller-Stach arXiv:1407.2388, Yoshinaga arXiv:0805.0349): absolutely convergent integral of a rational function with rational coefficients over a domain in ℝ^n given by polynomial inequalities with rational coefficients; complex numbers via real and imaginary parts. Coefficients are taken in ℚ (not ℚ̄), exactly as KZ do; the article notes the algebraic-coefficient variant is equivalent.

Domains are taken to be ℚ-semialgebraic sets (the Boolean algebra generated by {p ≥ 0}, p ∈ ℚ[x₁..xₙ]), following the careful literature (Huber–Müller-Stach; Commelin–Habegger–Huber arXiv:2007.08280 read KZ's 'real semi-algebraic set' this way). This includes finite systems of (strict or non-strict) polynomial inequalities as a special case and makes the ring property of periods unproblematic; a reviewer should confirm they accept this reading of 'given by polynomial inequalities'.

Absolute convergence is encoded as `MeasureTheory.IntegrableOn` (Lebesgue integrability) and the value as the Bochner set integral `∫ x in D, …` with respect to `volume` on `Fin n → ℝ` (product Lebesgue measure, checked via `volume_pi`).

The integrand `aeval x f / aeval x g` uses Lean's convention `r / 0 = 0`. If g ≠ 0 as a polynomial, its zero set is Lebesgue-null so nothing changes; if g = 0 the integrand is identically 0 and only produces the period 0, which is a period anyway. Hence the class of periods is unaffected.

The three conjectures are stated with the complex predicate `IsPeriod` applied to coerced real constants: `1 / π` elaborates to `1 / (↑Real.pi : ℂ)`, `exp 1` is `Real.exp 1` coerced, and `eulerMascheroniConstant` is `Real.eulerMascheroniConstant` coerced. `isPeriod_ofReal_iff` (proved) shows that for real numbers this is equivalent to being a real period.
Theorem names are exactly the slot ids (`exponential_periods.parts.i/ii/iii`) inside `namespace ExponentialPeriods`, as instructed; these are not Mathlib-style names.

Two auxiliary statements with complete proofs were added as `category test` / `category API` to sanity-check the definitions: every rational number is a real period, and `IsPeriod (a : ℂ) ↔ IsRealPeriod a`.

No definition of exponential periods is given, since the decomposition table contains no slot needing it (the 'which transcendental numbers are (exponential) periods?' question itself was dropped as non-statable). The module docstring records that e and γ are known exponential periods.

The definitions `IsRatSemialgebraic`, `IsRealPeriod`, `IsPeriod` are reusable and could be moved to `FormalConjecturesForMathlib/` in a real PR; they are kept in the problem file because the task restricts writes to the candidate file.
AMS tags `11 14` (number theory, algebraic geometry) were used for the three conjectures; the Wikipedia article is 'Period (algebraic geometry)'.

references.title: Euler's constant: Euler's work and modern developments

reviewer_notes: All eight candidates compiled and stated the same three propositions (1/π, e, γ are not Kontsevich–Zagier periods); the only substantive differences were in the bespoke period definition. Domain class: c01/c02/c08 use a single finite conjunction of weak inequalities {rᵢ ≥ 0} (basic closed sets). This is a narrower class than ℚ-semialgebraic sets and it is not obvious (nor established in the cited sources) that the resulting value set is closed under addition / equals 𝒫; a `¬ IsPeriod` statement over a possibly smaller class would be a weaker claim, so I preferred the Boolean-algebra reading used by the careful literature (Yoshinaga Def. 1 + semialgebraic sets, Commelin–Habegger–Huber Def. of k-semialgebraic sets, Lagarias 'equalities and inequalities'). c03/c04/c05/c07 all implement this Boolean-algebra reading equivalently (inductive predicate or `BooleanSubalgebra.closure`); c06 uses finite unions of finite intersections of {P ≥ 0}, which yields the same value set (strict inequalities differ by null sets) but is less standard. The `q ≠ 0` hypothesis in c01/c02/c03 is harmless but unnecessary (g = 0 gives the period 0; g ≠ 0 has null zero set), so it was not included. Verified: `volume` on `Fin n → ℝ` is `Measure.pi` by `rfl`; `IntegrableOn` encodes absolute convergence; n = 0 yields exactly the rationals (test lemma `isRealPeriod_ratCast` proven). Ambiguity in the original: the list entry 'Which transcendental numbers are (exponential) periods?' is an open-ended question with no statable Prop; per the decomposition table only the three concrete Kontsevich–Zagier non-period conjectures were formalized.
